messages.subject: Re: Comparing distance estimates
messages.body_plain:
Tony:

I can't speak to the Wilson Bulletin paper you cite, but presuming you
pool detections to get some sort of common detection function from which
to produce your detection probabilities, you have lost the independence
among your points, and they are not longer true replicates.

As an alternative, a forthcoming paper in the Journal of Biological and
Ecological Statistics speaks directly to your setup (burned/unburned
comparison, point transects, multiple years).  It is not yet in print,
but a preprint is posted on Prof. Buckland's website.

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202008.pdf

Roberts, Tony wrote:
> >      For my graduate work I am comparing densities of different bird species on burned and unburned grasslands where I surveyed avian communities using point counts over multiple years. Due to low numbers of detections per plot per species (<15) I am unable to get reliable density estimates for each plot using DISTANCE and needed to pool all detections to get a single density estimate. I cannot compare these two estimates using standard statistical techniques due to the log-normal distribution of the density estimate. Is there any formula or other type of test to be able to do this?
> >      I am thinking about trying methods used by Marcus et al. 2000 (Wilson Bulletin 112:517-523) with detection probabilities from DISTANCE. They used counts from each plot, also with low sample sizes, and divided those by detection probabilities then by the area surveyed. Then I can use individual plot density estimates and standard statistical tests. Thanks for any help, comments, or suggestions.

> >            Tony Roberts

messages.subject: DS in China ?!
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question to the list:

In the recent book by R. Harris (2008): Wildlife Conservation in China. M.E.
Sharpe, U.S.

it is stated (and somewhat criticized) that the government of China is
basically running nation-wide (!) Distance Sampling surveys as an inventory
method for their wildlife and biodiversity, e.g. in refuges.

To me, this sounds much better what Germany or many other western countries
achieve on that subject; wow.

I saw some of these surveys myself in a Chinese wildlife refuge; they were
done there during nesting and migration time.

However, I am amazed that this topic never comes up here on the listserver;
there must be huge questions (data and experiences) when running such a DS
program large-scale.

I would appreciate to hear more about these efforts, and from different
angles.
I think that this should be beneficial to us all, e.g. shared experiences.

Would you have some insights, or know details ?

Thanks so much in advance; yours

    Falk

Falk Huettmann PhD, Assistant Professor
-EWHALE lab- Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology
419 IRVING I, University of Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA
Email ff...@uaf.edu  Phone 907 474 7882 Fax 907 474 6716

messages.subject: Re: One Global detection function,
messages.body_plain:
Since your goal is to get area-time specific estimates, create 6 strata
with one for each area and time.  Use all of the data for a species or
group of species to estimate detection probability and then get
stratum-specific estimates of abundance by species.  Because they use
the same detection function across strata they will have covariances so
you'll have to deal with that but only if you want to combine them.  You
do have a couple of options here.
1) You can use CDS and use data filter to get the species (or species
group), fit the detection function (globally) and get stratum specific
abundance estimates.
That will work fine except for the species groups because you won't be
able to get density of each species within the group.
2) You can use MCDS and do the same as above but also consider area/time
or both as covariates to see if it is safe to assume that detection for
a species doesn't vary across time/area.  They same can be done with CDS
but is rather kludgy to do because you have to split out each data set
(species-area-time), fit the models, sum AICs and compare to AIC without
area-time.  But with CDS you can't fit additive models of area and time
and you can in MCDS.  Still the downside is that you still can't compute
species-specific estimates of abundance within a group of species pooled
to estimate the detection function.
3) You can use MRDS which was designed for double-observer surveys but
has a single-observer mode which is equivalent to MCDS with 2 big
differences. First, it will not use adjustment functions like with
CDS/MCDS. But, it will let you fit a common detection function to a
group of species and then get species-specific estimates within that
group by running a separate analysis that filters for each species and
then applies the common detection function. Additionally, it will output
the variance-covariance matrix of stratum specific estimates so you can
sum the estimates and construct the correct variance which is the sum of
the variances and covariances for the set being summed.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Re: One Global detection function,
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian, List,

I have another idea:

1. assign separate strata for each combination of area-time-species=20
2. filter for a given species group=20
3. fit a global detection function=20
4. estimate stratum-specific density estimates

The only difference from Jeff's option #2 is that strata include
species, in addition to area and time. Jeff reminded me to make sure you
correctly assign effort by area-time, regardless of species.

I'm planning on doing this same thing with my dataset, which sounds
similar to yours.  Feel free to contact me off list if you'd like to get
more into the gritty details.

Best,
Chris

Chris Merkord
University of Missouri
Columbia, MO, USA
clme...@mizzou.edu

messages.subject: Re: One Global detection function,
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian, List,

I have another idea:

1. assign separate strata for each combination of area-time-species=20
2. filter for a given species group=20
3. fit a global detection function=20
4. estimate stratum-specific density estimates

The only difference from Jeff's option #2 is that strata include
species, in addition to area and time. Jeff reminded me to make sure you
correctly assign effort by area-time, regardless of species.

I'm planning on doing this same thing with my dataset, which sounds
similar to yours.  Feel free to contact me off list if you'd like to get
more into the gritty details.

Best,
Chris

Chris Merkord
University of Missouri
Columbia, MO, USA
clme...@mizzou.edu

-----Original Message-----
From: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
[mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] On Behalf Of Jeff Laake
Sent: Wednesday, April 15, 2009 12:10 PM
To: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] One Global detection function, multiple levels
of stratification

Since your goal is to get area-time specific estimates, create 6 strata
with one for each area and time.  Use all of the data for a species or
group of species to estimate detection probability and then get
stratum-specific estimates of abundance by species.  Because they use
the same detection function across strata they will have covariances so
you'll have to deal with that but only if you want to combine them.  You
do have a couple of options here.
1) You can use CDS and use data filter to get the species (or species
group), fit the detection function (globally) and get stratum specific
abundance estimates.
That will work fine except for the species groups because you won't be
able to get density of each species within the group.
2) You can use MCDS and do the same as above but also consider area/time
or both as covariates to see if it is safe to assume that detection for
a species doesn't vary across time/area.  They same can be done with CDS
but is rather kludgy to do because you have to split out each data set
(species-area-time), fit the models, sum AICs and compare to AIC without
area-time.  But with CDS you can't fit additive models of area and time
and you can in MCDS.  Still the downside is that you still can't compute
species-specific estimates of abundance within a group of species pooled
to estimate the detection function.
3) You can use MRDS which was designed for double-observer surveys but
has a single-observer mode which is equivalent to MCDS with 2 big
differences.
First, it will not use adjustment functions like with CDS/MCDS. But, it
will let you fit a common detection function to a group of species and
then get species-specific estimates within that group by running a
separate analysis that filters for each species and then applies the
common detection function. Additionally, it will output the
variance-covariance matrix of stratum specific estimates so you can sum
the estimates and construct the correct variance which is the sum of the
variances and covariances for the set being summed.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Re: Comparison line transect and point transect
messages.subject_clean: Comparison line transect and point transect
messages.body_plain:
Johanna, I think the problem is more to do with the design than the
method.  You should get comparable abundance estimates - and you do,
when you take account of the very wide confidence interval for lines.
That is unsurprising, when you consider your design has just 3 lines.
That is far too few.  (In the 2001 book, we say 'a minimum of 10-20
lines'.)  If you can fit 72 points into your survey region, you can
certainly fit more than 3 lines in.

You should also use laser rangefinders, as measurement errors in point
transect sampling can generate substantial upward bias in the abundance
estimate - and your point transect abundance estimate is higher here
than your line transect estimate.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Johanna, I think the problem is more to do with the design than the
method.  You should get comparable abundance estimates - and you do,
when you take account of the very wide confidence interval for lines.
That is unsurprising, when you consider your design has just 3 lines.
That is far too few.  (In the 2001 book, we say 'a minimum of 10-20
lines'.)  If you can fit 72 points into your survey region, you can
certainly fit more than 3 lines in.

You should also use laser rangefinders, as measurement errors in point
transect sampling can generate substantial upward bias in the abundance
estimate - and your point transect abundance estimate is higher here
than your line transect estimate.

Steve Buckland
